opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is to stop treating memory as one flat thing. Today most long-context approaches basically say: keep every token, make attention cheaper, and hope the model finds the needle. But humans don't work that way. We forget most details, and that forgetting is actually a feature. It's a form of compression, and compression is close to understanding.

So if I were designing it, I'd think in layers. First, there's a short-term working memory, a window of recent tokens kept at full fidelity, where the model does precise reasoning. Second, there's a compressed memory. As information ages out of the window, the model shouldn't just drop it; it should summarize it into some latent state, something like what linear attention or state-space models do, where the history is folded into a fixed-size representation. That part is lossy by design. It keeps the gist, the structure, what mattered, and lets the surface details fade.

Third, and this is the part people often miss, you need an index back to the raw material. Forgetting in the compressed state is fine as long as you keep a pointer to where the details lived. It's like how you might not remember the exact sentence in a book, but you remember it was in chapter three, near the argument about something. So the compressed memory should carry retrieval keys, not just content. When the model realizes it needs a precise detail, a number, a name, a line of code, it issues a lookup and pulls the original segment back into working memory at full resolution.

The hard question is who decides what to forget and when to retrieve. I don't think hand-written rules will work. It should be learned, ideally with reinforcement learning, because the signal for "this detail was worth keeping" only shows up later, when the task succeeds or fails. That's a credit-assignment problem across long horizons, which is exactly what RL is for. You could even let the model take explicit memory actions, like writing a note, revisiting a passage, or discarding something, and train those actions end to end with the outcome.

There's also a nice side effect. If the model is forced to compress, it's forced to abstract. A system that keeps everything never has to decide what's important, so in a way it never really understands. A system that must forget has to build a model of the content. So I'd argue a good long-context design isn't about infinite memory. It's about good forgetting plus reliable recall, and the interplay between the two is where a lot of the intelligence comes from.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I've thought about a lot, because I think "forgetting" is actually the wrong framing to start from. People hear "long context" and immediately think the goal is to remember everything. But if you look at how any intelligent system actually works, including humans, the core ability isn't storage. It's compression with recoverability.

So let me describe how I'd approach it from first principles.

The first thing to recognize is that a long context has an enormous amount of redundancy. If you read a hundred pages of a document, most of what's in those pages is either predictable from the rest, or it's local detail that only matters for a short window. The information that genuinely needs to persist across the whole sequence is usually small. So the system shouldn't be trying to hold everything at full fidelity. It should be trying to hold a compressed state that preserves what's useful for the future, and that's a learned judgment, not a fixed rule.

The second thing, and this is where it gets interesting, is that "forgetting" and "retrieval" are not opposites. They're two halves of one design. If you have a good retrieval mechanism, you can afford to forget aggressively, because you know you can go back and get the detail when you need it. If you have no retrieval, you're forced to keep everything in working memory, and then the system becomes slow and the signal gets diluted. So I'd design it as a hierarchy. There's a small, high-bandwidth working state that gets updated continuously and compresses as it goes. Then there's a larger, cheaper store that keeps the raw material, or something close to it, and is only touched when the working state decides it needs something.

The hard part is the decision of when to go back. I don't think you want that to be a hand-designed heuristic. I think the model should learn it. The working state should carry some notion of uncertainty, of "I know there was something relevant here but I've lost the specifics," and that signal should trigger retrieval. That's actually how human memory feels, right? You don't remember a phone number, but you remember that you wrote it down and roughly where.

The third thing is about what gets compressed. I'd argue the compression should be semantic, not positional. A lot of current approaches throw away tokens based on how far away they are, or based on some attention score. That's a proxy. What you actually want is to keep abstractions and drop instantiations. Keep "this function validates the input and returns an error on failure," drop the exact variable names until you need them. This is also why I think the architecture should be allowed to summarize into its own internal representation rather than being forced to summarize into text. Text is a bottleneck. The model's native representation can hold a much richer, more useful compressed form.

And then the last point, which is more of a training question than an architecture question. You can't learn to forget well if your training signal only rewards remembering. Most long-context benchmarks are essentially needle-in-a-haystack tests, which push the model toward hoarding. If you want graceful forgetting, you need tasks where the cost of holding everything is real, where there's pressure to compress, and where the model is rewarded for recovering the right thing at the right time rather than for having never lost it. The behavior you want has to be in the objective.

So, to summarize the design: a compressed working state, a cheap long-term store, a learned signal for when to retrieve, semantic rather than positional compression, and a training setup that actually makes forgetting worthwhile. I think once you have those pieces, the length of the context stops being the interesting number. What matters is how well the system knows what it doesn't know.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate what the system keeps in its working context from what it can retrieve later. Forgetting something from the current context shouldn’t necessarily mean deleting it from memory.

You could have a small working context for the current task, a compressed summary of earlier interactions, and a searchable store of the original material. The summary preserves goals, decisions, and unresolved questions. Details can leave the working context, but the summary should retain pointers to where they came from.

When a new question arrives, the system retrieves relevant material and checks whether it actually supports an answer. That matters because compression can remove a qualification or turn an uncertain statement into something that sounds definite. Being able to return to the original passage helps prevent that.

The hard part is deciding what to forget. Recency alone isn’t enough: an old constraint may still matter, while a recent tangent may not. I’d make retention depend on the current task, expected future usefulness, and the cost of losing a detail. And I’d distinguish that from an explicit request to delete something, which should remove it from the underlying memory too.

Then I’d evaluate both sides: how much context we save, and how often the system can recover a necessary detail after a long gap. The goal is selective attention with reliable recall.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by separating what the system keeps in its active context from what it stores in memory. Those shouldn’t be the same thing. The active context should be small and focused on the current task; memory can be much larger, but it needs a retrieval mechanism.

Then I’d let the system forget at different rates. Exact wording and incidental details can fade quickly. Decisions, constraints, unresolved questions, and facts that keep being useful should persist longer. You can compress an old conversation into a summary, but that summary should retain pointers to the original passages. Otherwise, once you summarize away a detail, retrieval can’t bring it back.

When a new question arrives, the system first retrieves the relevant summaries, then follows those pointers if it needs more precision. And it should preserve uncertainty and provenance: who said something, when they said it, and whether a later statement replaced it.

The tricky part is that you don’t know in advance which detail will matter. So I’d make forgetting from active context cheap and reversible, while treating permanent deletion as a separate decision. Then I’d evaluate the system on whether it can recover the right evidence after long gaps—not just whether its summaries sound good.
